relative to the stars, but its speed varies far more dramatically than the Sun's, and the plane of its path is
tilted about five degrees to the ecliptic, with the crossing points themselves drifting westward and completing
a circuit in about 18.6 years. The five star-like planets present the hardest problem. Each generally moves
eastward against the stars, but each periodically slows, stops, reverses direction for weeks or months, stops
again, and resumes its eastward march. This is retrograde motion. Mars retrogrades for about seventy-two days
every twenty-six months; Jupiter for about a hundred and twenty days each year; Saturn for about a hundred and
forty days each year. Crucially, each planet is brightest in the middle of its retrograde loop, implying it is
then closest to us. Mercury and Venus behave differently again: they never stray far from the Sun, Mercury by at
most about twenty-eight degrees and Venus by about forty-seven, so they are only ever visible near dawn or dusk.
Finally the whole system drifts: the equinox points creep westward along the ecliptic at roughly one degree per
seventy-two years, a phenomenon called precession. These are the facts. A successful model must generate all of
them from geometry.

sections.heading: The Greek Inheritance: Eudoxus, Aristotle, Apollonius and Hipparchus
sections.body:
Ptolemy did not invent geocentric astronomy; he completed a project that had been running for five hundred
years. The founding constraint came from Plato and his circle in the fourth century before the common era: the
heavens are the realm of the perfect and unchanging, so celestial motion must be built from uniform circular
motion, since the circle is the only figure that returns on itself without beginning or end and uniform speed is
the only speed that requires no explanation. The task set to astronomers, in a phrase attributed to Plato, was
to save the appearances, meaning to reproduce the observed irregular motions using only combinations of uniform
circles. Eudoxus of Cnidus, around 370 before the common era, produced the first serious attempt: a system of
homocentric spheres, all sharing the Earth as centre, each rotating uniformly about an axis fixed in the sphere
outside it. By nesting three or four spheres per planet with carefully chosen axes and periods, Eudoxus could
generate a figure-of-eight path called the hippopede that reproduced retrograde motion qualitatively. His system
used twenty-seven spheres in total. Callippus improved it to thirty-four. Aristotle, wanting the spheres to be
real physical shells rather than a calculating device, added counter-rotating spheres to prevent each planet's
motion from being transmitted to the next, reaching fifty-five. Aristotle's contribution was less mathematical
than physical: in works such as On the Heavens he argued that the Earth is a sphere, that it sits at rest at the
centre of the cosmos because earthy matter naturally moves toward that centre, and that the heavens are made of
a fifth element, aether, whose natural motion is eternal circular rotation. This physics is what made geocentrism
compulsory rather than merely convenient, and it is why abandoning it later required a whole new theory of
motion. The homocentric system had a fatal flaw its own advocates noticed: because every sphere is centred on
the Earth, every body stays at a constant distance, so the model cannot explain why Mars grows about six times
brighter near opposition or why solar eclipses are sometimes total and sometimes annular. Around 200 before the
common era Apollonius of Perga supplied the fix by introducing eccentric circles and epicycles, and proved a
theorem showing the two devices are geometrically equivalent for the simplest cases. Hipparchus of Rhodes, active
around 150 to 125 before the common era and the greatest observational astronomer of antiquity, then used these
tools to build a quantitatively successful solar theory, a lunar theory, a star catalogue of over eight hundred
stars, and the discovery of precession. Hipparchus reportedly declined to build full planetary models, saying
the data were insufficient. Ptolemy inherited all of this, credited Hipparchus generously, and finished the job.

sections.heading: Claudius Ptolemy and the Almagest
sections.body:
Almost nothing is known about Ptolemy the man. He worked in or near Alexandria in Roman Egypt; his recorded
observations run from the ninth year of Hadrian, which is 125 or 126 of the common era, to about 141, and later
works push his activity to around 160 or beyond. The name Claudius suggests Roman citizenship and Ptolemy an
Egyptian or Macedonian connection, but no biography, no portrait and no reliable anecdote survives. What survives
instead is an extraordinary body of work: the astronomical treatise, a Geography that fixed the coordinates of
some eight thousand places and shaped mapmaking for a millennium, an Optics that studied refraction
experimentally, a Harmonics on musical intervals, and the Tetrabiblos, a systematic defence of astrology which he
regarded as the natural application of astronomy to terrestrial affairs. The astronomical work he called the
Mathematike Syntaxis, the Mathematical Compilation. Later Greek readers called it the Megiste Syntaxis, the
greatest compilation; Arabic translators rendered megiste as al-majisti, and Latin translators turned that into
Almagest, which is the name it has carried ever since. It is a large book, thirteen volumes in the conventional
division, and it is organised with the deliberate architecture of a textbook rather than the loose accumulation
of a commonplace book. Book one sets out the cosmological assumptions and develops the trigonometry needed for
everything that follows. Book two handles the consequences of the Earth's sphericity for observers at different
latitudes: lengths of day, rising times, shadow lengths. Book three presents the theory of the Sun. Books four
and five present the theory of the Moon, including the instrument he devised to measure lunar parallax. Book six
treats eclipses. Books seven and eight contain the star catalogue, with 1,022 stars in forty-eight
constellations, each with ecliptic longitude, latitude and a magnitude from one to six, a brightness scale still
in use in modified form today. Books nine through eleven build the models for the five planets in longitude,
book twelve treats retrogradation and greatest elongations, and book thirteen handles planetary latitude, the
motion of planets above and below the ecliptic, which is the hardest and least satisfactory part of the work.
Ptolemy's stated method is explicit and modern in tone: he states the phenomena, proposes the simplest geometric
hypothesis that might reproduce them, derives the parameters from a small number of carefully chosen
observations, and then constructs tables so that a reader can compute positions without repeating the geometry.
That last step mattered enormously. The Almagest is not merely an argument; it is a working computational
system, and its tables were still being used, corrected but not replaced, more than a thousand years later.

sections.heading: The Physical Cosmos: Sphericity, Centrality, and Immobility
sections.body:
Before any geometry, Ptolemy sets out five physical assumptions and defends each with an argument from
observation. First, the heavens are spherical and rotate as a sphere. His evidence is that the stars maintain
fixed relative positions while circling a pole, that circumpolar stars trace complete circles, and that stars
near the horizon are dimmed and displaced by the atmosphere as a spherical shell implies. Second, the Earth is a
sphere. Here the arguments are old and good: the pole star rises higher as one travels north, at a rate implying
a curved surface; travellers going east see a lunar eclipse at a later local hour than those in the west; a
ship's hull
disappears below the horizon before its mast; and the Earth's shadow on the Moon during a lunar eclipse is
always circular, which only a sphere casts from every orientation. Eratosthenes had already used the first
effect to measure the circumference at about 252,000 stadia, within a few per cent of the truth depending on
which stadion he meant. Third, the Earth is at the centre of the cosmos. Ptolemy's
argument is that the horizon always bisects the celestial sphere, since exactly six of the twelve zodiac signs
are above the horizon at any moment, and that this would fail if the observer were displaced from the centre.
Fourth, the Earth is a mere point relative to the sphere of the fixed stars, since no shift in the stars is
detectable between observations from different points on the Earth's surface. Fifth, the Earth does not move. Ptolemy's defence here is the most interesting passage in book
one, because it shows he had genuinely considered the alternative. He acknowledges that a rotating Earth would
explain the daily motion of the sky more simply and grants the astronomical appearances would be unchanged. His
objection is physical. If the Earth rotated, its surface would be moving eastward at enormous speed, and a stone
thrown straight up, or a bird released from a branch, would be left behind and fall to the west; clouds would
stream westward permanently. Nothing of the sort is seen. The objection is entirely correct given the physics
available to him; it is answered only by the principle of inertia, which was not formulated until Galileo and
Newton. The immobile Earth was a reasoned conclusion from empirical premises, and refuting it required
overturning the premises. In a later work, the Planetary Hypotheses, Ptolemy gave this cosmos actual dimensions
by assuming nature wastes no space, so each planet's spherical shell, thick enough to hold its epicycle at
nearest and farthest excursion, fits snugly inside the next. Anchoring on the Moon's measured parallax, between
about thirty-three and sixty-four Earth radii, he stacked upward to a Sun at 1,210 Earth radii and a sphere of
fixed stars at about 19,865, roughly a hundred and twenty million kilometres. That is twenty times too small for
the Sun alone. The scheme also fixed the planetary order outward from Earth as Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars,
Jupiter, Saturn, stars, an ordering still embedded in the names of the days of the week.

sections.heading: Deferents and Epicycles: The Basic Machinery
sections.body:
The central technical problem is generating non-uniform, sometimes backward, apparent motion from uniform
circular components. The epicycle solves it with elegant economy. Imagine a large circle centred on the Earth,
called the deferent, and imagine a point moving uniformly around it. Now attach a smaller circle, the epicycle,
centred on that moving point, and let the planet move uniformly around the epicycle. The planet's actual path is
the sum of two circular motions, and the resulting curve, depending on the ratio of radii and periods, can be a
looping figure that periodically carries the planet backward against the background of the stars. Retrograde
motion happens when the planet is on the inner part of its epicycle, moving opposite to the deferent's carrying
motion, and if the epicyclic speed there exceeds the deferent's, the net apparent motion reverses. Because the
planet is then also at its closest approach to the Earth, it is at its brightest, which is exactly what
observation shows. This single device therefore explains both retrogradation and the brightness variation that
had defeated the homocentric spheres. In modern terms, the epicycle is capturing a real physical effect: the
retrograde loop is a parallax phenomenon produced by the Earth overtaking a slower outer planet on the inside
track. The epicycle radius for an outer planet corresponds, in the heliocentric picture, to the radius of the
Earth's own orbit relative to the planet's. This is why the models worked so well; they encoded the correct
relative geometry, merely with the roles of Earth and Sun exchanged. There is a deep and important consequence.
Apollonius proved that a planet moving on an epicycle about a concentric deferent produces exactly the same
apparent motion as a planet moving on a single circle whose centre is offset from the Earth, provided the
parameters are matched. This eccentric-epicycle equivalence means the models are not unique; different
geometrical stories generate identical predictions. Ptolemy exploits this freedom, choosing whichever version is
computationally easier for each body, and he is explicit that he is choosing a hypothesis, not proving a
physical fact. It also means the frequent modern jibe about medieval astronomers piling epicycles upon epicycles
is largely a myth. Ptolemy uses one epicycle per planet, plus a second small circle for the Moon and a
supplementary device called the crank mechanism for Mercury. He does not stack epicycles indefinitely. The
picture of a system groaning under eighty or more circles comes from later composite versions and from
polemical caricature. The genuine complexity of the Ptolemaic system lies elsewhere, in the eccentric and the
equant, not in a proliferation of epicycles. It is worth noting the modern echo of this device. Any closed
periodic curve can be approximated arbitrarily well by summing enough circular motions of different radii and
frequencies, a result made rigorous in the nineteenth century as Fourier analysis. An epicyclic model is
literally a two-term Fourier series. That is why the technique is powerful, and why its power is a warning: a
scheme flexible enough to fit almost any curve tells you little about the cause of the curve.

sections.heading: The Eccentric and the Equant: Ptolemy's Decisive Innovation
sections.body:
Two further devices carry most of the accuracy of the system, and one of them is the point on which the whole
edifice was eventually attacked. The eccentric is simple: instead of centring the deferent on the Earth, place
its centre at a point offset from the Earth by some distance, conventionally written as e. A body moving
uniformly on such a circle appears from the Earth to move faster when it is on the near side and slower on the
far side, which reproduces a first-order speed anomaly without any epicycle at all. For the Sun, Ptolemy found
that a single eccentric circle with the offset equal to one twenty-fourth of the radius, that is e equal to
0.0417 in units where the deferent radius is 1, placed with its apogee at five and a half degrees of Gemini,
reproduced the observed lengths of the seasons. That model is accurate to a few arcminutes and remained in use
essentially unchanged for over a thousand years. In heliocentric terms it is capturing the real eccentricity of
the Earth's orbit, about 0.0167, doubled because the Ptolemaic construction absorbs the effect that Kepler would
later split between orbital eccentricity and the law of areas. For the planets, an eccentric alone was not
enough. The observed motion has a further asymmetry: the planet's angular speed and its distance do not vary in
step in the way a simple eccentric predicts. Ptolemy's solution was the equant, and it was radical. He placed
the Earth at distance e on one side of the deferent's centre, and then placed a second point, the equant point,
at distance e on the opposite side. The planet's carrying point then moves around the deferent circle at a rate
that is uniform as seen from the equant point, not from the circle's own centre. The motion is uniform about a
point that is not the centre of the circle it traverses. Geometrically this is a bisected eccentricity, and it
is an extremely good approximation. It reproduces Kepler's law of areas to first order in the eccentricity; the
error is of order e squared, which for the planets known to antiquity is small enough to be invisible to
naked-eye observation. The equant is the single most powerful idea in the Almagest. It is also, by the standards
of the tradition Ptolemy worked in, a violation. Uniform circular motion meant a body moving at constant speed
about the centre of its own circle. The equant preserves the appearance of uniformity while abandoning its
substance, and for the next thirteen centuries critics from Baghdad to Kraków would object that it was
geometrically effective but philosophically illegitimate.

sections.heading: The Solar Theory and the Measurement of the Year
sections.body:
The theory of the Sun is presented first because everything else depends on it: lunar theory needs solar
positions to predict eclipses, and every planetary model is tied to the Sun's motion. Ptolemy begins by
determining the length of the tropical year, the interval between successive spring equinoxes. He compares his
own equinox observations, made with a bronze ring set in the plane of the equator in the Alexandria palaestra, to
those of Hipparchus roughly 285 years earlier, and derives a year of 365 days plus a quarter minus one
three-hundredth of a day, about 365.24667 days. The true tropical year is 365.24219 days, so his figure is
roughly six and a half minutes too long, an error accumulating to about one day per 128 years, which over the
fourteen centuries the figure was in use contributed to the ten-day drift the Gregorian reform of 1582
corrected. The source of the error is instructive: Ptolemy trusted Hipparchus's long baseline, but his own
equinox timings appear systematically about a day late, probably from instrumental misalignment. Having fixed the year, Ptolemy determines the geometry from the
unequal lengths of the seasons. He takes the interval from spring equinox to summer solstice as 94 and a half
days and from summer solstice to autumn equinox as 92 and a half days. If the Sun moved uniformly on a circle
centred on the Earth, all four seasons would be equal at about 91.3 days each. From these two intervals he
solves for the eccentricity and the direction of apogee, obtaining e equal to 1/24 of the radius and an apogee
longitude of 65 and a half degrees. Notably, he treats this apogee as fixed relative to the equinoxes,
concluding from the agreement with Hipparchus that it does not move. In fact it does move, by about 1.7 degrees
per century relative to the fixed stars, so his solar apogee slowly became wrong; medieval Islamic astronomers,
notably al-Battani in the ninth century, detected the discrepancy and corrected it, which was one of the first
demonstrable improvements on the Almagest. The resulting solar table gives the equation of centre, the
correction between mean and true longitude, with a maximum value of two degrees and twenty-three minutes.
Applied properly, the model predicts the Sun's position to within about ten arcminutes, roughly a third of the
Sun's own apparent diameter. From this model Ptolemy also derives the equation of time, the varying difference
between apparent solar time as read from a sundial and uniform mean time as kept by a good clock. That
difference arises from two causes he handles separately: the Sun's non-uniform motion along the ecliptic, and
the obliquity of the ecliptic to the equator, which he measured as twenty-three degrees fifty-one and a third
minutes against a true value near twenty-three degrees forty-one minutes for his epoch. Without the equation of
time no sundial observation can be compared with any other, so this quiet piece of bookkeeping underwrites the
whole observational programme.

sections.heading: The Lunar Theory and the Crank Mechanism
sections.body:
The Moon is the hardest of the seven bodies, and Ptolemy's treatment of it is simultaneously his greatest
technical achievement and his most conspicuous failure. Hipparchus had already found a workable first
approximation: a simple epicycle model in which the Moon rides an epicycle whose centre travels around a
deferent, with the epicycle radius about one-thirteenth of the deferent radius. This reproduces the principal
inequality, now called the equation of centre, which reaches about six degrees and eighteen minutes and arises
from the real ellipticity of the Moon's orbit. Ptolemy verified this model against eclipse observations, where
the Moon is exactly opposite the Sun and its position is therefore known with unusual certainty, and found it
satisfactory at syzygy, meaning at new and full Moon. Then he did something no predecessor had done: he checked
it at quadrature, when the Moon is ninety degrees from the Sun, using his own careful observations with an
instrument he describes in detail, a pair of graduated rulers pivoted so as to measure a body's zenith distance,
which later writers called the Ptolemaic rulers or triquetrum. He found a large discrepancy, up to about two and
a half degrees, which no adjustment of the simple model could absorb. This is the second lunar inequality, the
evection, a genuine physical effect caused by the Sun's gravitational perturbation of the Moon's orbit and
amounting to about one degree sixteen minutes in modern terms. Ptolemy's solution was a mechanical device of
real ingenuity. He let the centre of the lunar deferent itself revolve around the Earth on a small circle, driven
by a crank arm that turned at twice the difference between the mean motions of the Moon and the Sun. The effect
is to pull the entire epicycle closer to the Earth at quadratures and push it away at syzygies, enlarging the
apparent size of the epicyclic correction exactly when the observations demanded it. Numerically it works
beautifully; the model predicts lunar longitude to within about ten arcminutes, good enough for eclipse
prediction. Physically it is a disaster, and Ptolemy knew it. The device makes the Moon's distance from the Earth
vary by nearly a factor of two, from about thirty-three Earth radii at perigee near quadrature to about
sixty-four at apogee. If that were true, the Moon's apparent diameter would double over the course of a month,
from roughly half a degree to a full degree, which is grossly contrary to observation; the real variation is only
about twelve per cent. Ptolemy never addresses this contradiction. It is the clearest case in the Almagest of a
model being tuned to fit one class of observation while flatly violating another, and it became the standard
example cited by later critics, from Ibn al-Shatir in fourteenth-century Damascus to Copernicus, that the system
required repair.

sections.heading: Models for the Five Planets
sections.body:
Books nine to eleven of the Almagest apply the full apparatus to Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus and Mercury, and
the structure is uniform enough to state once. Each planet has a deferent circle whose centre is offset from the
Earth by an eccentricity e, an equant point at distance 2e from the Earth on the far side, and an epicycle whose
centre is carried around the deferent at a rate uniform about the equant. Two periods govern the motion: the
period of the deferent, which is the planet's sidereal period, and the period on the epicycle, which is the
synodic period governing the retrograde cycle. Ptolemy determines the parameters from a small number of
carefully selected observations, typically three oppositions for an outer planet, since at opposition the
geometry simplifies. The critical structural
fact, which Ptolemy states but does not explain, is that the Sun is built into every planetary model. For the
outer planets, Saturn, Jupiter and Mars, the line from the epicycle centre to the planet always stays parallel to
the line from the Earth to the mean Sun, so the epicyclic period is exactly one year. For the inner planets,
Mercury and Venus, it is the deferent that is tied to the Sun: the epicycle centre sits permanently on the
Earth-Sun line and travels around in exactly one year, while the planet's own period is its orbital period, 88
days for Mercury and 225 for Venus, and the epicycle radius fixes the maximum elongation. This is why Venus never
appears more than about forty-seven degrees from the Sun. In heliocentric terms these coincidences are not
coincidences at all; every model contains a copy of the Earth's orbit, appearing as the epicycle for an outer
planet and as the deferent for an inner one. The Ptolemaic system was, in effect, carrying the correct answer
inside it in disguised form, which is precisely why Copernicus could reconstruct heliocentrism from Ptolemaic
parameters without any new observations. Mercury required special handling because its orbit is the most
eccentric of the classical planets, at 0.206, and because its greatest elongations are markedly unequal on
either side of the Sun. Ptolemy gave it a crank mechanism analogous to the Moon's, with the deferent centre
itself revolving on a small circle, producing two perigees rather than one. The model is contorted and its
accuracy is poor, with errors of several degrees, but Mercury is difficult to observe at all, never rising far
from twilight, so the failure went largely unpunished by the data. The overall performance of the planetary
theory deserves a plain statement, because it is often misrepresented. Modern recomputations show Ptolemy's
longitudes for Jupiter and Saturn are usually good to within about half a degree, Venus to about a degree, Mars
to a degree or two. A degree is twice the apparent width of the full Moon, and for predicting when a planet
would enter a zodiac sign that was entirely adequate.

sections.heading: Planetary Latitude, the Weakest Link
sections.body:
Everything discussed so far concerns longitude, motion along the ecliptic. But planets also move north and south
of the ecliptic, by up to about eight degrees in the case of Venus and Mercury and about two to seven degrees for
the outer planets, and this latitude motion is where the Ptolemaic system is at its worst. The underlying reality
is simple: each planet orbits the Sun in a plane slightly inclined to the Earth's orbital plane, by 1.85 degrees
for Mars, 1.30 for Jupiter, 2.49 for Saturn, 3.39 for Venus and 7.00 for Mercury, and these planes pass through
the Sun. Seen from a moving Earth, the resulting apparent latitude varies in a way that depends on where both
bodies are in their orbits. In a geocentric framework, with the Sun's role hidden, that behaviour has no natural
representation. Ptolemy's response in book thirteen is to tilt the deferent plane to the ecliptic and to tilt the
epicycle plane to the deferent, and then, because a fixed pair of tilts does not reproduce the observations, to
let the tilts themselves oscillate. He introduces what later writers called librations: the inclinations swing
back and forth in step with the planet's position, driven by small circles whose only justification is that they
make the numbers come out. For the inner planets he needs three separate components, which he names inclination,
obliquation and deviation. The resulting construction is by a wide margin the ugliest thing in the Almagest, and
Ptolemy's own later work, the Planetary Hypotheses, revises it substantially, which suggests he was not satisfied
either. Accuracy is correspondingly poor. Where his longitudes for Jupiter and Saturn are typically good to
within a degree or better, his latitudes can be wrong by a degree or more even for the outer planets, and the
inner planet latitudes are worse still. Later astronomers in the Islamic world and in Europe generally treated
latitude tables as the least trustworthy part of the inheritance, and it is telling that when Copernicus
reorganised the cosmos, latitude was one of the places where his system delivered an immediate and obvious
conceptual gain: the planes simply pass through the Sun, the tilts are constant, and the librations vanish
entirely as artefacts of the wrong reference point. This is a useful general lesson about theories. The
longitude models were accurate because they encoded correct relative geometry; the latitude models were bad
because there the geocentric framing had no correct geometry to encode, and only free parameters could bridge
the gap. When a theory needs new adjustable machinery for each new class of observation, while a rival explains
the same data by removing machinery, that asymmetry is real evidence, even though it is not a single decisive
experiment. Latitude was one of the first places where the two systems could be compared on those grounds rather
than on raw predictive accuracy, where for a long time they were nearly tied.

sections.heading: The Star Catalogue, Precession, and Instruments
sections.body:
Books seven and eight contain the oldest complete star catalogue to survive from antiquity: 1,022 stars grouped
into forty-eight constellations, each entry giving the star's position in ecliptic coordinates, longitude and
latitude, together with a magnitude on a six-point scale in which the brightest stars are first magnitude and the
faintest visible are sixth. That scale, formalised in the nineteenth century so that five magnitudes correspond
exactly to a hundredfold ratio in brightness, is still the standard photometric system in astronomy, which makes
it arguably the longest-lived measurement convention in any science. The forty-eight constellations, inherited
largely from earlier Greek tradition, form the core of the eighty-eight recognised today. The catalogue is
also the subject of the oldest genuine controversy in the history of astronomy. Because Ptolemy's longitudes can
be converted back to an earlier epoch by subtracting precession, several scholars from Tycho Brahe onward have
argued that the positions fit Hipparchus's era around 130 before the common era better than Ptolemy's own, and
that Ptolemy therefore copied Hipparchus's catalogue and simply added a constant. The astronomer Robert Newton
pressed this case forcefully in the 1970s in a book accusing Ptolemy of systematic fraud. Others, notably Owen
Gingerich and Bernard Goldstein, have argued that the discrepancies are better explained by Ptolemy's use of a
slightly too small precession constant and by his reliance on a small set of reference stars whose positions
carried systematic error. The honest position is that the question is not settled. What is clear is that Ptolemy
adopted a precession rate of one degree per century, whereas the true rate is about one degree per 71.6 years,
and that this error alone shifts positions by roughly one degree over the interval in question. Precession itself
he handles as a slow uniform rotation of the entire stellar sphere about the poles of the ecliptic, which is
geometrically the right description of the phenomenon even though its cause, the torque of the Sun and Moon on
the Earth's equatorial bulge, would not be understood until Newton. The instruments described in the Almagest
are worth knowing: a meridian quadrant of masonry for measuring the Sun's noon altitude and hence the obliquity;
an equatorial ring for timing equinoxes; the plinth, a graduated block with a pointer; the triquetrum for zenith
distances; and above all the armillary astrolabe, a nest of graduated rings representing the ecliptic, the
meridian and the horizon, which allowed a star's ecliptic longitude and latitude to be read directly by sighting
it against the Moon or a reference star. The practical precision of these devices was limited by the human eye's
resolving power, roughly one arcminute, and in practice by graduation errors and flexure to something closer to
five or ten arcminutes. That figure is the fundamental constraint on the whole enterprise: no geocentric or
heliocentric model could be tested beyond it until Tycho Brahe's instruments of the 1580s pushed the limit down
to one or two arcminutes, and the telescope after 1609 removed it altogether.

sections.heading: The Mathematics: Chords, Sexagesimals, and Tables
sections.body:
None of the astronomy is possible without a computational apparatus, and book one of the Almagest builds it from
scratch. Ptolemy did not have sines; Greek trigonometry worked with chords. The chord of an arc is the straight
line joining its endpoints in a circle of standard radius, which Ptolemy takes as sixty units. The relation to
the modern sine is exact and simple: chord of an angle theta equals 120 times the sine of half theta. He
constructs a table of chords for every half-degree from half a degree to a hundred and eighty degrees, giving
three sexagesimal places, which corresponds to about five decimal digits of precision. To build it he needs
chords of angles he can construct geometrically, which give him thirty-six degrees and seventy-two degrees from
the pentagon, sixty degrees from the hexagon, and ninety degrees from the square, together with half-angle and
difference formulae. The key tool is a result now called Ptolemy's theorem, which states that for any
quadrilateral inscribed in a circle, the product of the diagonals equals the sum of the products of the two
pairs of opposite sides. From this single theorem he derives what are effectively the addition and subtraction
formulae for sine and cosine. To get from ninety degrees down to a half-degree interval he needs the chord of one
degree, which is not constructible; he obtains it by a bounding argument, showing it lies between two computable
values that differ only in the third sexagesimal place, and takes the mean. That is a genuinely sophisticated
piece of numerical analysis. All arithmetic is done in the sexagesimal system inherited from Babylonian
astronomy, base sixty, which is why we still divide degrees into sixty minutes and minutes into sixty seconds,
and hours likewise. Sexagesimal fractions were vastly more convenient than the unit fractions of Egyptian
practice and gave Greek astronomers something close to a positional decimal system for fractional quantities
fourteen centuries before decimals reached Europe. Ptolemy also develops spherical trigonometry, relying on
Menelaus's theorem for the transversal of a spherical triangle, which lets him convert between ecliptic
coordinates, equatorial coordinates and the local horizon system for any latitude. Finally, and pedagogically
most important, he reduces every result to tables with interpolation rules. A user of the Almagest never repeats
the geometry; they look up a mean motion for the date, look up an equation in a table of corrections, add, and
obtain a position. This separation of derivation from routine computation is what made the system usable by
thousands of people who could not have reconstructed it, and it is the reason astronomical tables, rather than
astronomical arguments, became the working currency of the science for the next fourteen hundred years.

sections.heading: Transmission and Reform: Baghdad, Maragha, and Copernicus
sections.body:
The survival of Ptolemy's astronomy is a story of translation, and its reform is a story of purists. The Greek
text was copied in Byzantium and never entirely lost, but the living tradition of using and improving it moved
east. Under the Abbasid caliphs in Baghdad, and especially in the translation movement centred on the House of
Wisdom in the ninth century, the Syntaxis was rendered into Arabic at least four times, most influentially by
al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf around 827 and by Ishaq ibn Hunayn as revised by Thabit ibn Qurra later in that century. It
is from the Arabic al-majisti that the name Almagest derives. Islamic astronomers did far more than preserve.
Al-Battani, working at Raqqa around 900, found that the solar apogee had moved since Ptolemy's time, corrected
the tropical year to 365 days 5 hours 46 minutes 24 seconds, and refined the obliquity; his tables were still
cited by Copernicus six centuries later. Al-Sufi revised the star catalogue from fresh observation in the tenth
century and left the first recorded notice of the Andromeda nebula. Around 1028 Ibn al-Haytham wrote a book
titled Doubts Concerning Ptolemy, attacking the equant as physically incoherent: if the circles are real shells,
no rigid sphere can turn uniformly about an axis that misses its own centre. That objection drove the most
important reform programme in medieval astronomy. At the Maragha observatory in northwest Iran, around 1260,
Nasir al-Din al-Tusi devised the construction now called the Tusi couple, a small circle rolling without
slipping inside a circle of twice its radius, which converts two uniform circular motions into straight-line
oscillation. Mu'ayyad al-Din al-Urdi contributed the Urdi lemma, replacing an eccentric-plus-equant arrangement
with an equivalent pair of circles. Ibn al-Shatir, timekeeper at the Umayyad Mosque in Damascus around 1350,
assembled these into complete planetary models with no equant and no eccentric, using only concentric deferents
with secondary epicycles, and in the process fixed Ptolemy's lunar distance disaster. His models were still
geocentric. Latin Europe recovered the Almagest late and mostly through Arabic, in Gerard of Cremona's Toledo
translation of 1175, and worked from it through simplified textbooks and through the Alfonsine Tables compiled
under Alfonso X around 1272. The connection to Copernicus is one of the most striking findings in the history of
science: in the 1950s Otto Neugebauer and Edward Kennedy noticed that the planetary models of De Revolutionibus,
published in 1543, use the Tusi couple and the Urdi lemma and are mathematically identical to Ibn al-Shatir's,
differing only in the exchange of Earth and Sun. No channel of transmission has been documented, and scholars
remain divided between unrecorded influence and independent rediscovery. What is certain is that Copernicus's
stated motive matched the Maragha school's: he complained that Ptolemy's system violated uniform motion and was
a monster assembled from mismatched parts. For him heliocentrism restored an ancient principle rather than
overthrowing it, and his system used about as many circles and was no more accurate.

sections.heading: Working With the System: Reading a Ptolemaic Prediction
sections.body:
It is worth seeing concretely how a person actually used this machinery, because the abstraction hides how
practical it was. Suppose a fourteenth-century astronomer in Oxford wants the longitude of Mars for a given
night. He does not draw circles. He opens a set of tables and performs a fixed arithmetic routine, summarised
below in modern language. The whole calculation takes perhaps fifteen minutes with practice and needs nothing
but addition, subtraction and linear interpolation between tabulated values, all in sexagesimal degrees and
minutes. Interpolation error of a few arcminutes is immaterial when the model itself is only good to a degree.
The same routine serves for any planet; the Moon needs an extra step for the crank correction and the Sun only
the first three steps. A skilled practitioner could produce a year's ephemeris for all seven bodies in a few
weeks, and the sale of such ephemerides, mostly for astrological purposes such as casting nativities and
choosing dates for medical procedures, is what paid for astronomy through the medieval period. That economic
fact explains why the discipline survived, why Ptolemy wrote the Tetrabiblos as a companion volume, and the
shape of the profession: demand was for reliable numbers on a schedule, not for understanding, and a system that
delivered them had enormous inertia regardless of its physical truth.
steps: Find the mean longitude of the planet for the date. Take the tabulated mean longitude at a fixed epoch, usually the beginning of the reign of Nabonassar in 747 before the common era, and add the tabulated mean motion for the elapsed years, months, days and hours.
Find the mean anomaly, the planet's mean angular position on its epicycle, by the same method from its own table of mean motion in anomaly.
Subtract the longitude of the deferent apogee from the mean longitude to obtain the mean centre, the angle measured at the equant point from apogee to the epicycle centre.

Enter the table of the equation of centre with the mean centre and read the first correction. Apply it with the tabulated sign to obtain the true centre, the actual direction from Earth to the epicycle centre.
Apply the same correction to the mean anomaly to obtain the true anomaly, the planet's real angular position on the epicycle measured from the direction of the epicycle apogee as seen from Earth.
Enter the table of the equation of anomaly with the true anomaly to read the second correction, which represents the planet's displacement from its epicycle centre as seen from Earth.

Because that displacement depends on how far away the epicycle currently is, scale the second correction using the interpolation coefficient tabulated against the true centre, which ranges between the values at greatest and least distance.
Add the scaled equation of anomaly to the true longitude of the epicycle centre. The result is the planet's true ecliptic longitude for the date.
If the date is after Ptolemy's epoch by more than a century or two, add the accumulated precession at one degree per hundred years to convert from his fixed-star frame to the tropical frame in use.

sections.heading: How the System Ended, and What Its Failure Teaches
sections.body:
The geocentric cosmos did not fall to a single crucial experiment, and understanding how it actually ended
corrects a great deal of popular mythology. Copernicus's book of 1543 changed nothing immediately: its
predictions were no better than the Alfonsine tables it replaced, and it faced physical objections its author
could not answer. For sixty years the common professional position was to use Copernican mathematics as a
superior calculating device while denying its physical truth. Four developments settled matters over the
following century. Tycho Brahe's observations from Uraniborg between 1576 and 1597 pushed positional accuracy
from roughly ten arcminutes to one or two, making the residual errors of both systems visible for the first
time, while his study of the 1572 supernova and the 1577 comet showed that change occurs above the Moon and that
a comet's path must cut straight through the crystalline shells. Kepler, working on Tycho's Mars data, found in
1605 that no combination of circles fitted within eight arcminutes, and in 1609 replaced deferent and equant
with an ellipse and the law of equal areas, cutting free parameters while improving accuracy tenfold. Galileo's
telescope between 1609 and 1611 produced facts the old cosmos could not hold, above all the complete cycle of
phases of Venus, which is impossible if Venus rides an epicycle between Earth and Sun. Newton's Principia of
1687 finally supplied the missing physics: inertia explained why a moving Earth is not felt, and gravitation
explained why the ellipses are there at all. The absent stellar parallax that Ptolemy had cited was measured
only in 1838, when Bessel found 61 Cygni shifting by about a third of an arcsecond, a hundred times below any
pre-telescopic instrument. The geocentrists were not careless; the effect really is that small. Set out plainly,
the system's failures fall into three classes. Parametric errors were merely wrong numbers, such as the year six
and a half minutes too long or the precession constant a quarter too small, and every one was found and fixed
inside the geocentric framework, which is evidence the tradition was functioning as science. Local structural
failures were places the geometry could not represent the phenomenon at all, notably a lunar distance varying
twofold against a twelve per cent variation in apparent diameter. The foundational failure was that the system
had no dynamics: it could say where a planet would be but never why, could not connect celestial to terrestrial
motion, and had no way of being surprised. The practical use of all this is diagnostic. Ptolemy's theory fitted
the data, so fitting the data proves little. Ask instead whether a theory needs new adjustable machinery for
each new class of observation, whether its parameters conceal coincidences it cannot explain, such as every
planetary model secretly containing the same annual cycle, and whether it can tell you why as well as what.

guides.title: Islamic and Medieval Astronomy
guides.summary: A survey of astronomy between the eighth and sixteenth centuries: how Greek, Indian and Persian learning was absorbed and transformed in the Islamic world, the instruments, tables, observatories and planetary models that resulted, the parallel Latin tradition, and what this long period actually contributed to the science that followed.

sections.heading: Why the Medieval Centuries Matter
sections.body:
There is a popular story in which astronomy is invented by the Greeks, falls asleep for a thousand years, and wakes up with Copernicus. It is wrong in almost every particular. The eight centuries between the death of Ptolemy around 170 and the publication of Copernicus in 1543 were among the most productive in the history of the subject, and the overwhelming majority of that work was done in Arabic, in a scientific culture stretching from Córdoba to Samarkand, with a smaller but genuine parallel tradition in Latin Europe, in Hebrew, and in Byzantine Greek.

The scale is easy to underestimate. Several thousand Arabic manuscripts on astronomy survive, many still unedited. Hundreds of astronomical handbooks with tables, the genre called the zij, were compiled between the ninth and sixteenth centuries. Observational programmes at Baghdad, Cairo, Maragha, Samarkand and Istanbul produced parameters more accurate than Ptolemy's by an order of magnitude in some cases. Instruments were refined to a standard of workmanship that has never been surpassed by hand. Trigonometry as a distinct mathematical discipline, with the sine, tangent and cotangent and the spherical relations that govern them, was essentially created in this period because astronomy demanded it.

It is equally important not to overcorrect into a triumphalist story in which medieval astronomers secretly anticipated everything. They did not discover heliocentrism, though several discussed it and set it aside for reasons that were serious rather than stupid. They did not develop the telescope, and their observational accuracy remained bounded by the naked eye at roughly one to two minutes of arc at best. They worked within a geocentric cosmology inherited from Aristotle and Ptolemy and, with a small number of exceptions, sought to repair it rather than replace it.

What they did do was more subtle and, in the long run, more consequential. They subjected Ptolemy to sustained technical criticism, identified precisely where his models violated the physical principles they were supposed to embody, and constructed alternative geometrical devices that removed those violations while preserving the predictions. Those devices, above all the pair of nested rotating circles known as the Tusi couple, reappear in the work of Copernicus in forms so specific that historians have argued about the transmission for seventy years. They also established astronomy as an institutional activity with funded observatories, salaried staff, long observational programmes and the expectation that tables would be checked and corrected, which is a research culture rather than a collection of individual insights.

Understanding this period properly requires holding two facts together: that it was a genuine continuation and extension of Greek science rather than mere preservation, and that it remained within a framework that would eventually have to be abandoned.

sections.heading: The Inheritance: Greek, Indian and Persian Sources
sections.body:
Astronomy in the early Islamic world drew on three distinct traditions, and much of its early history is the story of reconciling them.

The Greek inheritance was dominated by one book. Ptolemy's Mathematical Syntaxis, written in Alexandria around 150 and known to the Arabic world and thence to Europe as the Almagest, from al-majisti, the Arabic rendering of the Greek for the greatest, was a complete mathematical astronomy: a star catalogue of 1,022 entries, geometrical models for the Sun, Moon and five visible planets, tables for computing their positions, and the trigonometry needed to use them. Alongside it came Ptolemy's Planetary Hypotheses, which set out a physical arrangement of nested spheres, his Handy Tables, Euclid's Elements, and the works of Aristotle that supplied the underlying physics of a stationary Earth at the centre of a universe of concentric celestial spheres made of an unchanging fifth element.

The Indian inheritance arrived earlier and by a different route. According to a well-known account, an Indian delegation reached the court of the caliph al-Mansur in Baghdad around 771 carrying a Sanskrit astronomical treatise, probably related to the Brahmasphutasiddhanta of Brahmagupta, which was translated into Arabic as the Sindhind. Indian astronomy brought computational methods, a different set of parameters, and above all the sine function, which the Greeks did not use. Ptolemy worked with chords, the straight line joining the ends of an arc; Indian astronomers worked with the half-chord, which is the sine, and this is much more convenient. It entered Arabic as jayb and passed into Latin as sinus, which is why the modern term means a fold or bay.

The Persian inheritance came from the Sasanian empire, whose astronomers had produced a royal handbook known as the Zij-i Shah, itself a blend of Greek and Indian material. It carried a strong astrological orientation and a distinctive system of very long planetary periods.

A fourth strand deserves mention because it is often left out. Pre-Islamic Arabian folk astronomy had its own well-developed body of knowledge, organised around the anwa, the risings and settings of particular stars that marked the agricultural and meteorological year, and around the twenty-eight lunar mansions through which the Moon passes in a month. This tradition was practical, calendrical and entirely non-mathematical, and it persisted alongside the learned tradition for centuries, supplying much of the vocabulary of star names and remaining the astronomy that ordinary people actually used.

These three learned traditions did not agree. Their parameters for the length of the year, the rate of precession and the positions of the planetary apogees differed measurably, and their computational styles were incompatible. The earliest Arabic astronomical works, such as the zij of Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi in the early ninth century, are visibly hybrid, using Indian methods with Greek geometry and Persian parameters. The intellectual work of the ninth century was to determine which system was right, and the answer, reached through fresh observation, was that Ptolemy's geometry was superior but his numbers needed correcting.

sections.heading: Translation, Patronage and the House of Wisdom
sections.body:
The transmission of Greek science into Arabic was not an accident of proximity. It was a sustained, expensive, state-supported programme lasting roughly two centuries, and it has few parallels in history.

The Abbasid caliphs moved their capital to the newly founded Baghdad in 762, into a region where Greek, Syriac, Persian and Sanskrit learning already circulated. Under al-Mansur, Harun al-Rashid and above all al-Ma'mun, who reigned from 813 to 833, translation became a matter of state policy. The institution associated with this effort, the Bayt al-Hikma or House of Wisdom, is often described as a great research academy, and here honesty is required: the surviving evidence is thin, and modern scholarship, notably that of Dimitri Gutas, argues that it was probably a library and translation bureau of modest scale rather than the university-like institution of popular accounts. The translation movement itself, however, is beyond doubt, and its scale is documented in the bibliographies of the period.

The translators were often Syriac-speaking Christians whose communities had preserved Greek learning. Hunayn ibn Ishaq and his son Ishaq ibn Hunayn were the most celebrated, working with a methodological care that included collating multiple Greek manuscripts to establish a better text. Thabit ibn Qurra, from the Sabian community of Harran, was both translator and original mathematician. The Almagest was rendered into Arabic more than once, first by al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf around 827 and later in a superior version by Ishaq ibn Hunayn revised by Thabit.

Crucially, translation was accompanied immediately by verification. Al-Ma'mun commissioned fresh observations at Baghdad and at Damascus explicitly to test Ptolemy's parameters, and the resulting set of tables was known as the Verified Tables. His astronomers measured the obliquity of the ecliptic, the tilt of Earth's axis relative to its orbit, obtaining about 23 degrees 33 minutes against Ptolemy's 23 degrees 51 minutes; the true value for the ninth century was near 23 degrees 35 minutes, so the new measurement was far better. Al-Ma'mun also sponsored a geodetic expedition to the plain of Sinjar which measured the length of one degree of latitude by direct survey, obtaining a figure implying an Earth circumference within a few per cent of the modern value.

That combination, translating a text and then testing it against the sky rather than treating it as authority, is the defining methodological feature of the tradition and the reason it produced new science rather than commentary.

The motives behind the patronage were mixed, and it is worth being plain about them. Some were intellectual and some were religious, since astronomy served the determination of prayer times, the direction of prayer and the lunar calendar. A great deal, however, was astrological. Rulers wanted horoscopes cast, elections of auspicious moments for military campaigns and the founding of cities, and predictions of dynastic change, and accurate astrology requires accurate planetary positions. Much of the funding that produced the best observational astronomy of the age was justified by an enterprise that turned out to have no predictive value whatever.

sections.heading: The Ptolemaic System and Its Machinery
sections.body:
To understand what medieval astronomers were arguing about, one must understand the machine they inherited, because nearly every technical dispute for eight centuries concerns one of its components.

The problem Ptolemy solved was this. Planets do not move uniformly. They speed up and slow down against the stars, and periodically they reverse direction entirely for weeks or months before resuming, a phenomenon called retrograde motion. Since Plato, Greek astronomy had accepted as a principle that celestial motion must be uniform and circular, because the heavens were held to be perfect and unchanging. The task was to reproduce the observed irregularity using only combinations of uniform circular motions.

Ptolemy used three devices. The first is the eccentric: instead of placing Earth at the centre of a planet's circular path, displace it slightly, so that the planet appears to move faster when nearer and slower when further. The second is the epicycle: the planet moves on a small circle whose centre rides around a larger circle called the deferent. When the epicyclic motion carries the planet backwards relative to its deferent motion, retrograde motion results. The combination of eccentric and epicycle can reproduce a great deal.

The third device was the one that caused eight centuries of trouble. To match observation accurately, Ptolemy found he had to allow the centre of the epicycle to move at a rate that was uniform not about the centre of the deferent, and not about the Earth, but about a third point called the equant, placed on the opposite side of the deferent centre from the Earth and at an equal distance. Mathematically this works beautifully; the equant is in fact an excellent approximation to the effect of the elliptical orbit and varying speed that Kepler would describe in 1609.

Philosophically it was a scandal. If a planet is carried by a real physical sphere, that sphere must rotate uniformly about its own axis, through its own centre. A sphere that turns uniformly about a point that is not its centre is not turning uniformly at all; some part of it must speed up and slow down, which the physics of the celestial element forbade. The equant therefore violated the very principle the whole system existed to uphold.

Ptolemy also left the Moon in an unsatisfactory state. His lunar model matched the observed longitudes well, but it required the Moon's distance to vary by nearly a factor of two over each month, which would make its apparent diameter vary by the same factor. Anyone who looks at the Moon can see that it does not. This discrepancy, obvious to any careful observer, became the standard opening move of every serious critique.

sections.heading: The Zij: Astronomical Tables as the Central Genre
sections.body:
If one wants to know what a medieval astronomer actually spent his working life producing, the answer is usually a zij. The word denotes an astronomical handbook with tables, and more than two hundred distinct examples are known from the Islamic world alone. A zij was the practical instrument of the science, and it is a genre with no close modern equivalent: part reference work, part manual, part set of computational algorithms encoded as numbers.

A typical zij opens with chronology, giving the rules for converting between the several calendars in simultaneous use, which might include the Islamic lunar calendar, the Persian solar Yazdgird era, the Syrian and Byzantine calendars and sometimes the Coptic. It then supplies trigonometric tables, sines and tangents at intervals of a degree or finer. The heart of the work is the planetary tables: for each body, the mean motions over days, months, years and multiples of years, together with tables of the corrections, called equations, that convert the mean position into the true one. There follow tables for parallax, for solar and lunar eclipses, for the visibility of the lunar crescent, for the rising times of the signs of the zodiac at a given latitude, a star catalogue giving positions and magnitudes, and finally geographical coordinates for major cities, since almost every calculation depends on latitude and longitude.

The arithmetic was sexagesimal, that is base sixty, inherited from Babylon through the Greeks. This is why an hour still has sixty minutes and a degree sixty minutes of arc. Positions were routinely tabulated to two or three sexagesimal places, corresponding to a resolution of a second of arc, which was a great deal finer than anything actually observable and reflects the demands of iterated computation rather than any claim to that accuracy.

The important zijes trace the development of the science. The Sindhind zij of al-Khwarizmi in the early ninth century is hybrid and Indian in method. The Sabi zij of al-Battani, working at Raqqa around the year 900, is a landmark: he redetermined the solar parameters from his own observations, discovered that the direction of the Sun's apogee had shifted since Ptolemy's time, which is a real effect, gave the length of the tropical year as 365 days 5 hours 46 minutes 24 seconds, and abandoned chords for sines. The Hakimi zij of Ibn Yunus at Cairo around 1000 preserves a long series of carefully dated eclipse observations that modern astronomers have used to study the slowing of Earth's rotation. The Ilkhani zij from Maragha and the Sultani zij of Ulugh Beg from Samarkand mark the culmination of the tradition. Zijes also travelled and were adapted: the Toledan Tables compiled in eleventh-century Spain were carried into Latin Europe, translated, and remained in use for two centuries before being superseded by the Alfonsine Tables produced at Toledo around 1272 under Alfonso X of Castile, which themselves survived until the sixteenth century.

sections.heading: The Astrolabe and How It Was Used
sections.body:
The planispheric astrolabe is the emblematic instrument of the period, and it deserves its reputation: it is an analogue computer that solves, by rotating a disc, a large class of problems in spherical astronomy that would otherwise demand laborious trigonometry.

Its principle is stereographic projection, known to the Greeks and described by Ptolemy. Imagine the celestial sphere with an observer inside it. Project every point of that sphere from the south celestial pole onto the plane of the equator. This projection has a remarkable property: every circle on the sphere maps to a circle on the plane, which means the horizon, the meridian, the circles of equal altitude and the daily paths of the stars all become drawable circles. The instrument is that drawing, made in brass.

A complete astrolabe has a body called the mater, hollowed to hold a stack of flat plates. Each plate, or tympan, is engraved with the projected horizon, zenith, altitude circles known as almucantars and azimuth lines for one specific latitude, so a traveller carried several. Above the plate sits the rete, a pierced openwork disc which is a map of the sky: an eccentric circle representing the ecliptic and a set of pointers whose tips mark named bright stars. The rete rotates over the plate exactly as the sky rotates over the landscape. On the back are scales of degrees, a calendar relating date to solar position, shadow squares for surveying, and a pivoting sighting arm called the alidade.
steps: Determine your latitude and select the tympan engraved for it, or the nearest available; an error of more than a degree or two noticeably degrades results.
Suspend the astrolabe by its ring so it hangs freely and vertically, and stand out of the wind.

Sight the Sun or a known star along the alidade, for the Sun by letting a sunbeam pass through the pinhole of the upper vane onto the lower rather than by looking at it, and read the altitude in degrees off the outer scale on the back.
Turn the instrument over. Using the calendar scale on the back, find the Sun's position in the zodiac for today's date.

Rotate the rete until the marker for that solar position, or the pointer for the star you sighted, lies exactly on the almucantar circle matching the altitude you measured, choosing the eastern side before local noon and the western side after.

Lay the rule across from the centre through that same point and read the hour off the scale around the rim; this gives local time, in unequal hours if the plate is so marked or in equal hours if it is not.

Without moving the rete, read off the altitude and azimuth of every other star on the instrument, the portion of the ecliptic then rising, and the times of sunrise and sunset, since one setting of the rete answers all of these at once.

sections.heading: Quadrants, Armillary Spheres and Giant Instruments
sections.body:
The astrolabe was portable, versatile and, precisely because of that, limited in accuracy. Its scales are small, so a reading finer than about five or ten minutes of arc is not achievable. Serious observational programmes therefore used instruments built to a different philosophy: fixed, massive and above all large, because angular precision on a graduated arc improves in direct proportion to the radius.

The quadrant, a quarter circle graduated in degrees with a plumb line or sights, existed in many forms. The simple horary quadrant, small enough for a pocket, gave the time from a solar altitude for one latitude. The sine quadrant, or rub al-mujayyab, carried a grid of lines that allowed trigonometric functions to be read off mechanically and was the standard working tool of the professional mosque timekeeper. At the other extreme, mural quadrants were built into masonry walls aligned exactly north to south, with radii of several metres, and used to measure the meridian altitude of the Sun and stars with great precision.

The armillary sphere was a skeletal model of the celestial sphere made from graduated metal rings representing the equator, ecliptic, meridian and horizon. Fitted with sights it became an observing instrument for measuring celestial longitude and latitude directly, and unfitted it served as a teaching model. Ptolemy had described such an instrument, and Islamic astronomers built larger and better versions.

The most distinctive achievement was the deliberate pursuit of size. The parallactic ruler, the triquetrum, and the great mural sextants were built at scales that had no precedent. The most famous example is the Fakhri sextant at Ulugh Beg's observatory in Samarkand, constructed in the 1420s: a segment of a meridian arc with a radius of about forty metres, sunk into a trench cut in the bedrock so that it could be rigid. At that radius, one minute of arc corresponds to about twelve millimetres on the arc, which can be read comfortably by eye. This is the reasoning that later drove Tycho Brahe to build his own large instruments, and it represents a genuinely modern understanding that precision is an engineering problem.

Two other instruments deserve note. The equatorium was a mechanical device of discs and pointers that computed planetary positions geometrically without arithmetic, effectively a physical model of the Ptolemaic mechanism. Water clocks and, from the fourteenth century, mechanical clocks in Europe began to provide independent timekeeping, which matters because until then time itself was usually measured astronomically, making certain observations circular.

The honest limit on all of this is the human eye. The resolving power of unaided vision is about one minute of arc for a person with excellent sight, and in practice, with sighting vanes rather than telescopic sights, systematic errors of two to five minutes were normal even on the largest instruments. Enlarging an instrument beyond a point buys nothing, because flexure, thermal expansion, imperfect graduation and the difficulty of aligning a sight begin to dominate. The best medieval positions are roughly comparable with Tycho Brahe's late sixteenth-century work, and both stand at the ceiling of what is possible without optics.

sections.heading: Observatories as Institutions
sections.body:
One of the period's most consequential inventions was not an instrument or a theory but an institution: the observatory as a funded, staffed, long-term establishment with a research programme, a library and a director.

The earliest were the ninth-century programmes at Baghdad and at Damascus under al-Ma'mun. These were organised efforts with named participants and a stated goal, the verification of Ptolemy's parameters, but they did not long outlive their patron. The tradition matured over the following centuries in Cairo, Isfahan, where Omar Khayyam worked on calendar reform in the 1070s producing a solar year good to within seconds, and Toledo, where al-Zarqali and his colleagues compiled the Toledan Tables that later dominated Latin Europe.

The turning point was Maragha, in north-western Iran, founded in 1259 under the patronage of the Ilkhanid ruler Hulagu with Nasir al-Din al-Tusi as director. Maragha was an institution on a new scale: a large library, an endowment, a staff of astronomers drawn from across the Islamic world and reportedly including a Chinese scholar, and an observational programme deliberately planned to run for thirty years so that the slowest planetary cycles could be covered. Saturn takes about twenty-nine and a half years to complete one circuit, so a thirty-year programme is precisely what a rigorous determination of its motion requires. The observatory produced the Ilkhani zij and, more importantly, became the centre of the theoretical work that reformed planetary theory.

Samarkand followed in the 1420s under Ulugh Beg, a Timurid prince who was himself a capable working astronomer, an unusual combination. Its Sultani zij of 1437 contained a star catalogue of 1,018 stars whose positions were newly observed rather than copied from Ptolemy with a precession correction applied, the first substantial catalogue since antiquity to be genuinely independent. Its parameters were superb: the sidereal year to within about a minute of the true value, the obliquity of the ecliptic to 23 degrees 30 minutes 17 seconds.

The Istanbul observatory of Taqi al-Din, founded in 1577, illustrates the fragility of the institution. Well equipped and productive, it was demolished in 1580 on the order of the sultan after political and religious opposition, only three years after it opened. The pattern is common: observatories depended on the personal support of a ruler, and they rarely survived his death or a change of political mood. Maragha declined within decades; Ulugh Beg was murdered in 1449 and his observatory was abandoned and eventually lost, its site rediscovered only in 1908. Against that fragility must be set what the model achieved. The idea that astronomy requires a permanent establishment rather than a gifted individual with a private instrument, that observations should be systematic and dated and archived for successors, and that a programme should be planned around the periods of the objects studied, all descend from this tradition and pass through Tycho's Uraniborg into the modern research observatory.

sections.heading: Doubts About Ptolemy
sections.body:
Criticism of Ptolemy was not a late development or a marginal opinion. It ran continuously from the ninth century onward and became the central theoretical preoccupation of the science.

The critics were careful to distinguish two questions. Did the models predict planetary positions accurately? Broadly yes, within the accuracy then attainable. Were they physically coherent as descriptions of real rotating spheres? Here the answer was clearly no, and the discipline that addressed this was called ilm al-hay'a, the science of the configuration, a genre of works concerned with the physical arrangement of the heavens as distinct from the computational tables.

Ibn al-Haytham, known in Latin as Alhazen and better remembered for founding modern optics, wrote around 1030 a work whose title translates as Doubts Concerning Ptolemy. It is a model of technical criticism. He argued that Ptolemy's models, whatever their predictive merits, could not correspond to any real arrangement of bodies, because the motions they required were impossible for solid spheres. The equant was his principal target: a sphere cannot rotate uniformly about a point other than its own centre without tearing itself apart or ceasing to be uniform. He also attacked the lunar model on the observational ground that the predicted variation in the Moon's distance was flatly contradicted by the constancy of its apparent size. His conclusion was not that Ptolemy was worthless but that the configuration of the heavens had not yet been correctly determined, and that this was the outstanding problem of the science.

In al-Andalus a different and more radical response emerged. Ibn Bajja, Ibn Tufayl and Ibn Rushd, the philosopher known in Latin as Averroes, argued on Aristotelian grounds that epicycles and eccentrics were unacceptable in principle, since all celestial motion must be about the centre of the universe. Al-Bitruji, Latinised as Alpetragius, attempted around 1200 to build an entirely homocentric system with all spheres centred on Earth. It was philosophically pure and predictively hopeless, failing to reproduce even the gross features of planetary motion, and its failure is instructive: it demonstrated that the Aristotelian requirement and observational adequacy could not both be satisfied within the geocentric framework.

Al-Biruni, writing in the early eleventh century, went further than most in one respect. He recorded that the question of whether Earth rotates on its axis could not be settled by astronomical observation, since the appearances would be identical either way, and he discussed the arguments seriously before setting the idea aside on physical grounds. This is not a suppressed anticipation of Copernicus. It is something more interesting: a clear-eyed recognition of what the available evidence could and could not decide. The physical objection to a moving Earth was not superstition either. If Earth turned, why did a stone dropped from a tower not land behind its base, and why was there no perpetual east wind? Answering those questions required a new mechanics, which arrived only with the concept of inertia, and until it did, a stationary Earth was the position the evidence supported.

sections.heading: The Maragha Solutions: the Tusi Couple and Its Relatives
sections.body:
The critics had shown what was wrong. The astronomers of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries built the mathematical devices to fix it, and this body of work is the most technically impressive achievement of the period.

The central invention is the Tusi couple, described by Nasir al-Din al-Tusi in his Memoir on Astronomy of 1261. Take a circle, and inside it place a second circle of exactly half its diameter, touching internally. Roll the small circle around the inside of the large one, and simultaneously rotate the small circle about its own centre at twice the rate in the opposite sense. Under these conditions a point on the circumference of the small circle traces not a curve but a straight line, oscillating back and forth along a diameter of the large circle. This is a genuinely beautiful result, provable by elementary geometry, and its significance is that it generates linear oscillation out of nothing but uniform circular motions. Every irregularity that Ptolemy had produced by illegitimate means could now be produced by legitimate ones.

Mu'ayyad al-Din al-Urdi, working at Maragha alongside Tusi, contributed a second device now called the Urdi lemma, which allows an eccentric motion to be replaced by an equivalent arrangement of two circles. Qutb al-Din al-Shirazi, Tusi's student, applied these tools systematically to build full planetary models free of the equant.

The culmination came a century later and in a different city. Ibn al-Shatir was not a court astronomer but the muwaqqit, the professional timekeeper, of the Umayyad Mosque in Damascus, where he died around 1375. In a work titled The Final Quest Concerning the Rectification of Principles, he constructed complete models for the Sun, Moon and planets that dispensed entirely with the equant and with eccentric deferents, using only combinations of epicycles centred on the Earth. His lunar model solved the distance problem that had troubled everyone since Ibn al-Haytham, producing a variation in the Moon's apparent size that matched what the eye actually sees.

It is important to be clear about what these models were and were not. They remained geocentric. They were not simpler than Ptolemy's; in several cases they required more circles. They did not predict noticeably better. What they did was satisfy the physical requirement that every motion be uniform about the centre of its own sphere, which was, within the accepted framework, exactly the right thing to demand. They represent the geocentric system pushed to its highest state of internal consistency, and in that sense they mark the end of a road rather than the opening of a new one.

The mathematics, however, outlived the cosmology entirely. A device that converts uniform circular motion into linear oscillation is useful to anyone building a kinematic model, and the Tusi couple was later put to work by astronomers who had abandoned the Earth-centred universe altogether. Good mathematics is portable in a way that good cosmology is not.

sections.heading: Religious Practice as an Engine of Precision
sections.body:
A distinctive feature of astronomy in the Islamic world is that three religious obligations generated demand for exactly the kind of mathematical precision that pure theory alone might not have sustained.

The first is the qibla, the direction of Mecca, which a worshipper faces during prayer and toward which mosques are oriented. Determining it correctly is a serious problem in spherical trigonometry: given the latitude and longitude of your location and of Mecca, find the azimuth of the great circle joining them. This is not a matter of pointing roughly south-east; it is the solution of a spherical triangle, and it demands the spherical law of cosines or an equivalent. Approximate folk methods existed and were widely used, but from the ninth century onward astronomers including Habash al-Hasib, al-Biruni and later al-Khalili produced exact solutions and universal tables. Al-Khalili, in fourteenth-century Damascus, tabulated the qibla for every degree of latitude and longitude difference, some three thousand entries, each a spherical triangle solved by hand.

The second is the five daily prayers, whose times are defined by the position of the Sun: dawn twilight, midday just after the Sun crosses the meridian, the afternoon prayer defined by the length of a gnomon's shadow relative to its noon length, sunset, and nightfall. These definitions depend on latitude and season, so tabulating them for a city across the year is a substantial exercise. From the thirteenth century the response was institutional: mosques employed a muwaqqit, a salaried astronomical timekeeper, whose job was to determine prayer times, maintain instruments and often to teach. Ibn al-Shatir held such a post, and the fact that the most sophisticated planetary theorist of the fourteenth century was employed as a mosque timekeeper says a great deal about how the science was supported.

The third is the lunar calendar. The Islamic month begins with the first visibility of the new crescent after conjunction, and predicting that is genuinely difficult, since it depends on the angular separation of Sun and Moon, the Moon's altitude at sunset, atmospheric clarity and the observer's eyesight. Astronomers developed visibility criteria of increasing sophistication, rules stating the minimum arc between Sun and Moon required for the crescent to be seen, and these are the ancestors of the criteria still debated today.

The result was a body of applied spherical astronomy of great practical accuracy, and a professional class of astronomers with steady employment independent of princely whim, which is one reason the science survived the collapse of individual observatories.

The demand also drove pure mathematics. Solving these problems required trigonometry, and the trigonometry available from the Greeks was inadequate. Abu al-Wafa, in late tenth-century Baghdad, established the spherical law of sines and computed sine tables accurate to eight decimal places. Al-Tusi's Treatise on the Complete Quadrilateral, written at Maragha, is the first work to present trigonometry as an independent discipline rather than a servant of astronomy. Jamshid al-Kashi at Samarkand computed the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter to sixteen decimal places in 1424, a record that stood for nearly two centuries.

sections.heading: Observation, Star Catalogues and the Names We Still Use
sections.body:
Alongside the theory ran a continuous programme of observation, and its residue is visible in the modern sky in a way most people never notice: several hundred of the bright stars are known by names that are Arabic, often mangled by transliteration through Latin.

The key text is the Book of the Fixed Stars, completed by Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi at Isfahan in 964. It is a critical revision of Ptolemy's catalogue rather than a copy: al-Sufi checked positions and magnitudes against his own observations, corrected errors, and gave for each constellation two drawings, one as seen on a celestial globe and one as seen in the sky, mirror images of one another.
