A curved mirror, however, focuses light by reflection, which treats all colors identically; a telescope built around a mirror would be free of color error in principle. In 1668 Newton, a skilled hands-on experimenter, cast, ground and polished a small mirror of speculum metal, an alloy of roughly two parts copper to one of tin, figured it to focus, and built around it a telescope about six inches long with a mirror of just over an inch, magnifying about 35 times, performing, he claimed, like a refractor several feet long. His second instrument, sent to the Royal Society in London at the end of 1671, caused a sensation, secured his election as a Fellow in January 1672, and prompted his first published paper, on light and colors.

Newton's layout, still called the Newtonian, solved the reflector's geometric puzzle, that the observer's head would block incoming light, with a small flat secondary mirror set diagonally near the top of the tube, deflecting the converging beam out the side to an eyepiece mounted at right angles. He was not alone in the field of ideas: the Scottish mathematician James Gregory had published a two-mirror design in 1663, with a pierced primary and a small concave secondary reflecting light back through the hole, but contemporary opticians could not figure its curves, and a working Gregorian waited decades. In 1672 the Frenchman Laurent Cassegrain proposed the variant with a convex secondary, which folds a long focal length into a short tube; dismissed by Newton at the time, the Cassegrain geometry is, ironically, the ancestor of most large telescopes today, including the Hubble Space Telescope.

The reflector's promise was real, but its material betrayed it for a century. Speculum metal takes a fine polish and was the only mirror surface available, glass could not yet be silvered, but it reflects only about two thirds of the light even when fresh, and it tarnishes: months of damp air dull the surface, and repolishing risks ruining the optical figure, so a serious observer needed spare mirrors and endless labor. The alloy is also brittle as porcelain and heavy. Consequently the early eighteenth century belonged to craftsmen who could manage these vices: notably John Hadley in London, whose six-inch Newtonian of 1721 was the first reflector genuinely to rival the long aerial refractors, tested head-to-head by the Royal Society against a 123-foot Huygens lens and found comparable, in a tube six feet long. Hadley also devised practical tests of mirror figure during polishing, the beginning of optical shop testing.

By mid-century, makers such as James Short of Edinburgh had turned Gregorians into a commercial product, hundreds of neat brass instruments for gentlemen's libraries and for the transit-of-Venus expeditions of 1761 and 1769. The reflector thus established itself as the compact, color-free alternative, always brighter in promise than in tarnishing practice, while the refractor awaited its own redemption. That came from an unexpected direction: a quiet English barrister who wondered whether Newton's incurable disease was curable after all.

sections.heading: The Achromatic Lens: Chester Moore Hall, John Dollond and the Refractor Reborn
sections.body:
Newton's declaration that chromatic aberration was incurable rested on an experimental conclusion that refraction and dispersion, the bending of light and the spreading of its colors, were locked in fixed proportion in all materials. That conclusion was wrong, and the man who first acted on its wrongness was Chester Moore Hall, an English barrister of Essex with a private passion for optics. Around 1729 Hall reasoned that different glasses disperse color differently: crown glass, the common window and spectacle material, spreads the spectrum less for a given bending than the dense, lead-rich flint glass developed for cut crystal. Pair a strong convex lens of crown with a weaker concave lens of flint, and the flint's stronger color-spreading can cancel the crown's while only partly undoing its focusing power. The compound lens focuses light, and brings red and blue to very nearly the same point: an achromatic doublet.

Hall had such lenses made around 1733, and, wanting secrecy, farmed the two elements to two different London opticians, both of whom, the story runs, subcontracted to the same craftsman, George Bass, who thus quietly learned the secret. Hall never published or patented; a few small achromatic telescopes existed almost invisibly for two decades. The idea reached consequence through John Dollond, a Spitalfields silk weaver turned optician of Huguenot descent, who learned of the crown-flint combination, repeated and extended the experiments rigorously, presented his results to the Royal Society in 1758, receiving its Copley Medal, and took out a patent on the achromatic lens that same year. His son Peter Dollond, a sharper businessman, enforced the patent vigorously against the London trade; rival opticians protested that Hall was the true inventor, and a court agreed he was first, but upheld the patent for Dollond as the one who had brought the invention to the public benefit, a legal judgment still quoted in patent law. Peter Dollond went on to add a third element, the triple achromat of 1763.

The achromatic doublet re-founded the refractor. Color error shrank by an order of magnitude, so focal lengths could collapse: a three-foot achromat outperformed the thirty-foot simple lenses of the previous century, and telescopes returned indoors, onto steady brass mounts, into observatories and ships' cabins. The remaining barrier was raw material: flint glass could not be cast free of striae, internal veins, in disks much beyond ten centimeters, so early achromats stayed small. The breakthrough came from the Swiss artisan Pierre-Louis Guinand, who around 1805 learned to stir molten glass with a fireclay rod, homogenizing the melt, and who took his secret to the Munich workshop where Joseph von Fraunhofer worked. Fraunhofer joined superb glass to something new: measurement. Using the dark solar spectral lines he catalogued in 1814, the Fraunhofer lines, he measured refractive indices precisely and designed doublets by calculation rather than trial.

His masterpiece, the 24-centimeter Dorpat refractor delivered to Wilhelm Struve in 1824, was the finest telescope in the world and introduced the equatorial mount with clock drive, one axis aligned to the celestial pole so a weight-driven mechanism could follow the stars automatically, the pattern for every major telescope for a century. With it Struve measured over three thousand double stars, and in 1838, with a Fraunhofer-tradition instrument, Friedrich Bessel measured the first stellar parallax, the distance to the star 61 Cygni, about eleven light-years. The reborn refractor had begun surveying the universe's third dimension, and it was about to grow very large indeed.

sections.heading: William Herschel: Giant Reflectors and the Discovery of Uranus
sections.body:
William Herschel arrived at astronomy sideways. A Hanoverian military bandsman's son who settled in England in 1757, he made his living in Bath as an organist, composer and music teacher, and took up astronomy in his thirties with an ambition unusual among amateurs: not to admire the planets but to survey the whole construction of the heavens, which demanded light grasp no shop-bought instrument could supply. So he built his own, teaching himself to cast and polish speculum mirrors, sometimes grinding for sixteen hours at a stretch while his sister Caroline read to him and fed him, and by the late 1770s his homemade Newtonians, notably a 6.2-inch reflector of seven feet focal length, were sharper than the instruments at Greenwich.

With that seven-foot telescope, on the night of 13 March 1781, from his garden at 19 New King Street in Bath, Herschel was methodically examining stars in Gemini when he noted one that showed a disk. He first announced it as a comet, but its slow motion and computed orbit, nearly circular and far beyond Saturn, revealed within months something unprecedented: a new planet, the first ever discovered, doubling the radius of the known solar system at a stroke. Herschel proposed naming it Georgium Sidus for King George III; the international community settled eventually on Uranus. The reward was a royal pension that let him quit music, move near Windsor, and become, with Caroline, a full-time astronomer.

Herschel's program was the deep sky. With a twenty-foot telescope of 18.7 inches aperture, completed in 1783, he and Caroline swept the heavens systematically for two decades, cataloguing about 2,500 nebulae and clusters where fewer than 150 had been known, the catalogue that grew into today's NGC, while Caroline, observing on her own account with a small sweeper telescope, discovered eight comets between 1786 and 1797 and became the first woman paid for scientific work in England. Herschel counted stars in hundreds of sample fields to map the Milky Way's shape, concluding it was a flattened stratum, a grindstone, with the Sun inside, the first observational model of our galaxy. He discovered two moons of Saturn, Mimas and Enceladus, in 1789, and two of Uranus, Titania and Oberon, in 1787; comparing star catalogues, he demonstrated in 1783 that the Sun itself moves through space toward a point in Hercules; and in 1800, testing thermometers placed beyond the red end of the solar spectrum, he discovered infrared radiation, the first light invisible to the eye.

His largest instrument taught a different lesson. The forty-foot telescope, finished in 1789 with royal money, carried a 48-inch speculum mirror weighing about a ton, the largest telescope on Earth for half a century and a tourist marvel. But the great mirror tarnished relentlessly, flexed under its own weight, and the unwieldy altazimuth scaffold made observing slow; Herschel used it far less than his twenty-foot, and its chief discoveries, Mimas and Enceladus, came in its first weeks. The forty-foot became astronomy's standing caution that aperture without usability is spectacle rather than science. Yet the direction was set: Herschel had shown that the reflector was the instrument of the deep sky, that the universe of nebulae was vast and unexplored, and that one determined builder could out-instrument every national observatory on Earth. The next such builder took the hint to an Irish castle.

sections.heading: The Leviathan of Parsonstown and the Discovery of Spiral Nebulae
sections.body:
William Parsons, third Earl of Rosse, applied an aristocrat's resources and an engineer's temperament to a single question: what are the nebulae? At his seat, Birr Castle in County Offaly, Ireland, he spent the 1830s and 1840s reinventing speculum-mirror technology at scales nobody had attempted, training local workmen, building steam-driven grinding and polishing machines, and devising a mirror alloy and casting practice that could survive cooling without cracking, itself a feat, since a large speculum disk shatters if cooled unevenly, and his three-foot blanks were annealed in ovens for weeks.

After a successful 36-inch telescope, Rosse committed to a mirror of six feet, 72 inches, in diameter. Two four-ton blanks were cast, ground to a focal length of 54 feet, and mounted in 1845 in a tube nearly 60 feet long slung between two masonry walls seventy feet long and about fifty high, aligned north-south. The walls braced the tube against wind, at the price of motion: the Leviathan of Parsonstown, as it was promptly nicknamed, could swing freely only in altitude along the meridian, with just a degree or so of sideways play, so an object was observed for the hour it took the sky to carry it through the slot. Observers rode galleries high above the ground in the Irish night; the largest telescope in the world until 1917 never had a clock drive, a photographic plate, or a dome.

It hardly mattered, because eyes at the eyepiece of a six-foot mirror saw what no one had seen. In the spring of 1845, examining the nebula catalogued as Messier 51 in Canes Venatici, Rosse discerned that it was wound into a spiral, a whirlpool of luminous coils with a companion knot, and his drawing of the Whirlpool Nebula, reproduced across Europe, is one of astronomy's iconic images; Vincent van Gogh's Starry Night is widely thought to echo it. The Leviathan went on to resolve spiral structure in more than a dozen nebulae, to resolve parts of others into swarms of stars, and to show that the nebular sky was structured, dynamic, various. Rosse also named the Crab Nebula, from an 1840s drawing made with the 36-inch.

The spirals sharpened the deepest question in nineteenth-century astronomy without settling it. Were the nebulae comparatively nearby clouds within our star system, perhaps planetary systems condensing, or were they, as Immanuel Kant had speculated in 1755, island universes, entire galaxies like the Milky Way at immense distances? Resolution into stars argued one way; the discovery by William Huggins in 1864, with a spectroscope on a refractor, that some nebulae show the bright-line spectrum of glowing gas argued the other, and the debate would not close until 1924. The Leviathan itself, magnificent and nearly immovable, marked both the summit and the end of the speculum age: its mirrors demanded repolishing, its light was hostage to Irish weather, and after Rosse's death in 1867 and his son's astronomical career, the great telescope fell silent in the 1890s, was dismantled but never scrapped, and was restored at Birr in the 1990s with a new aluminum-coated mirror, where it stands today. The future belonged to two better technologies already maturing: the giant achromatic refractor, and glass mirrors coated with silver.

sections.heading: The Great Refractors: Clark Lenses from Dearborn to Yerkes
sections.body:
The second half of the nineteenth century was the refractor's imperial age. Guinand's and Fraunhofer's glassmaking advances matured in the works of Chance Brothers in England and Feil and Mantois in Paris, which could at last cast flint and crown disks tens of centimeters across; and a family firm in Cambridgeport, Massachusetts, Alvan Clark and Sons, became the world's finishing school for giant lenses. Alvan Clark, a portrait painter turned optician, and his sons George Bassett and Alvan Graham, figured objective after record-breaking objective, testing on double stars, and five times in succession the world's largest refractor carried Clark glass.

The sequence itself tells the story. In 1862, testing a new 18.5-inch objective destined for Chicago's Dearborn Observatory, Alvan Graham Clark pointed it at Sirius and saw beside the Dog Star a faint companion in exactly the position celestial mechanics had predicted: Sirius B, the first white dwarf ever seen, whose existence Friedrich Bessel had inferred in 1844 from Sirius's wobbling motion. In 1873 the firm delivered the 26-inch for the United States Naval Observatory in Washington, with which Asaph Hall discovered the two moons of Mars, Phobos and Deimos, in August 1877. Then came 30 inches for Pulkovo in Russia in 1883, and in 1888 the 36-inch for the new Lick Observatory on Mount Hamilton in California, the first great mountain-summit observatory, where the steady air validated a principle every later builder followed: site matters as much as size. With the Lick refractor, E. E. Barnard discovered Amalthea in 1892, the first new moon of Jupiter since Galileo's four.

The culmination was Yerkes. George Ellery Hale, a young solar astronomer with matchless gifts for persuasion, learned in 1892 that two 40-inch glass disks, cast for a failed Southern California project, were available, and talked the Chicago streetcar magnate Charles Tyerson Yerkes into funding the world's largest telescope around them. The Yerkes Observatory at Williams Bay, Wisconsin, dedicated in 1897, mounted the Clark-figured 40-inch objective, a metric meter of glass, in a 63-foot tube on a German equatorial mount within a ninety-foot dome, with a rising floor to bring observers to the eyepiece. It was, and remains, the largest refracting telescope ever put into regular astronomical service.

It was also the end of its line, for reasons Yerkes itself demonstrated. A lens can be supported only around its edge, since light must pass through it, and a 40-inch, quarter-ton doublet sags measurably under its own weight, flexing as the telescope tracks; glass thick enough to resist absorbs light; and the residual secondary spectrum of even the best doublet smears photographic blue light, just as photography was becoming astronomy's principal detector. A mirror, by contrast, can be supported across its whole back, reflects all colors identically, and needs one perfect surface rather than four. Every argument that had once favored lenses now favored silvered glass. Hale understood this before Yerkes was finished; the observatory's optical shop was soon at work on a 60-inch mirror blank his father had bought him, and Hale himself, the greatest telescope entrepreneur in history, had already turned his eyes toward a mountain in Southern California called Wilson's Peak. The refractor had carried astronomy to the threshold of the galaxies; mirrors would carry it through.

sections.heading: Glass Mirrors and Mountaintops: Mount Wilson, Hubble's Universe and Palomar
sections.body:
Two nineteenth-century inventions dethroned speculum metal. In 1856-57, Karl August von Steinheil and Leon Foucault independently applied Justus von Liebig's chemistry for depositing silver from solution onto glass: a glass mirror, ground and polished once, could now be coated with silver reflecting over ninety percent of visible light, and recoated in an afternoon whenever it tarnished, without touching the optical figure. Foucault added the knife-edge test, which reads a mirror's figure to fractions of a wavelength with equipment costing pennies. Glass reflectors grew quickly respectable, and in George Ellery Hale's hands, imperial.

Having built Yerkes, Hale moved to Mount Wilson above Pasadena, founding the solar observatory there in 1904 with Carnegie money. The 60-inch reflector, its blank bought by his father years before, saw first light in 1908 and was the most powerful photographic telescope on Earth; with it Harlow Shapley, studying variable stars in globular clusters, showed by 1918 that the Milky Way was vastly larger than assumed and that the Sun sat tens of thousands of light-years from its center, a second Copernican demotion. Hale was already fundraising past it: the Los Angeles businessman John D. Hooker paid for a 100-inch disk, cast in wine-bottle green glass by Saint-Gobain in France, so bubbled that Hale's opticians despaired before concluding the bubbles did not reach the polished face. The Hooker telescope began work in November 1917 and was the largest telescope in the world for over thirty years.

On its platform the scale of the universe was settled. In October 1923 Edwin Hubble, photographing the Andromeda Nebula with the 100-inch, identified a Cepheid variable star, a class whose pulsation period reveals its true luminosity, thanks to Henrietta Swan Leavitt's period-luminosity law of 1912, and the Cepheid's faintness placed Andromeda around a million light-years away, far outside any conceivable Milky Way. The island-universe debate, formally staged between Shapley and Heber Curtis in 1920, was over: the spirals Rosse had sketched were galaxies. Hubble pressed on, and in 1929, combining his distances with the galaxy redshifts Vesto Slipher had been measuring since 1912, announced that recession velocity rises in proportion to distance, the observational cornerstone of the expanding universe.

Hale had one more telescope in him. Securing six million dollars from the Rockefeller Foundation in 1928, he launched the 200-inch project: a Pyrex blank, low-expansion glass ribbed like a waffle to halve its weight, cast by Corning in New York in December 1934 after a first flawed attempt, cooled for ten months, shipped cross-country by special train, and polished in Pasadena for a decade around the war. Mounted on Palomar Mountain in a horseshoe equatorial that let it cross the pole, the Hale Telescope was dedicated in June 1948, ten years after Hale's death, and reigned as the world's largest effective telescope until the 1990s. Its mirrors, like all modern ones, wore not silver but aluminum, applied in vacuum by a process perfected by John Strong in the 1930s, more durable and better in the ultraviolet. With the 200-inch, Walter Baade doubled the cosmic distance scale in 1952 by sorting out two populations of Cepheids, and Allan Sandage spent a career measuring the expansion. Astronomy now lived on mountaintops, and its next instruments would leave the ground entirely, in two directions at once: toward radio wavelengths, and toward space.

sections.heading: Radio Telescopes: Listening to the Sky from Jansky to the Event Horizon Telescope
sections.body:
The radio sky was discovered by accident, in the service of the telephone. In 1932 Karl Jansky, a young engineer at Bell Telephone Laboratories in Holmdel, New Jersey, was tracing sources of static troubling transatlantic radiotelephone links, using a rotating antenna array at 20.5 megahertz mounted on Model T wheels, his colleagues called it the merry-go-round. Among thunderstorm crackles he isolated a steady hiss that peaked not every 24 hours with the Sun but every 23 hours 56 minutes, the sidereal day, the fingerprint of a source fixed among the stars. By 1933 he had located it in Sagittarius, toward the center of the Milky Way. Bell had its answer, reassigned him, and professional astronomy, almost unbelievably, ignored the result for years.

The field was kept alive by one man in his backyard. Grote Reber, a radio engineer in Wheaton, Illinois, built a 31-foot parabolic dish behind his mother's house in 1937, the first true radio telescope, and by the early 1940s had mapped the radio Milky Way, finding bright regions in Sagittarius, Cygnus and Cassiopeia and publishing, after initial bafflement from referees, in the Astrophysical Journal. Wartime radar then trained a generation and left surplus equipment everywhere, and after 1945 radio astronomy erupted, especially in Britain and Australia. At Jodrell Bank in Cheshire, Bernard Lovell built the 250-foot fully steerable Mark I dish, completed in 1957, financially rescued in the public eye when it proved the only instrument in the West able to track Sputnik's carrier rocket by radar. At Cambridge, Martin Ryle developed aperture synthesis, combining many small, movable antennas so that Earth's rotation sweeps them into the equivalent of one vast dish, work that won the 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics, shared with Antony Hewish, whose Cambridge array had detected, through graduate student Jocelyn Bell's vigilance in 1967, the clockwork pulses of the first pulsar.

Radio astronomy's discoveries remade physics. The 21-centimeter line of neutral hydrogen, predicted in 1944 and detected in 1951, mapped the Galaxy's spiral arms through dust no optical telescope could pierce. Quasars, starlike radio sources revealed in 1963 to lie at cosmological distances, unveiled supermassive black holes; the cosmic microwave background, found in 1965 by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson with a horn antenna a few miles from Jansky's old site, fixed the hot Big Bang; pulsar timing yielded the first evidence for gravitational waves. The instruments grew commensurately: the 305-meter fixed spherical dish at Arecibo, Puerto Rico, built in a karst sinkhole in 1963, was the largest single telescope on Earth until China's 500-meter FAST opened in 2016; Arecibo's platform collapsed in December 2020 after cable failures, ending an era. The Very Large Array in New Mexico, dedicated in 1980, spread 27 25-meter dishes along a Y of rail track with arms 21 kilometers long, synthesizing images sharper than optical telescopes of its day.

The technique's extreme is very long baseline interferometry, recording signals at dishes on different continents against atomic clocks and correlating them later, making a virtual telescope the size of the Earth. Its signature achievement came in April 2019, when the Event Horizon Telescope collaboration, eight millimeter-wave observatories from Hawaii to the South Pole, published the first image of a black hole's shadow, the ring of hot gas around the 6.5-billion-solar-mass black hole in the galaxy Messier 87, followed in 2022 by the black hole at our own galaxy's center, the source in Sagittarius where Jansky's hiss began.

sections.heading: Telescopes in Space: Hubble, the Great Observatories and the James Webb
sections.body:
Earth's atmosphere is a problem a mountaintop only softens: its turbulence smears starlight, it glows faintly, and it is opaque to most of the electromagnetic spectrum, all gamma rays and X-rays, nearly all ultraviolet and most infrared. The astrophysicist Lyman Spitzer spelled out the remedy in a 1946 report, decades before it was feasible: put a large telescope in orbit. Small ultraviolet and X-ray satellites of the 1960s and 1970s, and the X-ray pioneer Uhuru in 1970, proved the case, and NASA committed to a flagship: the Hubble Space Telescope, a 2.4-meter Cassegrain reflector, carried into orbit by shuttle Discovery on 24 April 1990.

Within weeks came disaster verging on farce: stars focused not to points but to fuzzy halos. The primary mirror, exquisitely polished, had been polished to precisely the wrong shape, its edge too flat by about two microns because a testing instrument had been assembled with a spacing error, giving textbook spherical aberration. The rescue turned Hubble into legend. Because the flaw was perfectly characterized, corrective optics could cancel it, and Hubble had been designed for orbital servicing: in December 1993 the crew of shuttle Endeavour installed COSTAR's corrective mirrors and the aberration-corrected WFPC2 camera in a series of spacewalks, and the restored images were flawless. Four further servicing missions through 2009 replaced instruments, gyroscopes and batteries, leaving Hubble more capable in its third decade than its first, still working past its thirty-fifth year.

Hubble's harvest justified every dollar several times over: the deep fields, staring at blank sky to reveal thousands of galaxies reaching back over thirteen billion years; Cepheid measurements that pinned the universe's expansion rate near seventy kilometers per second per megaparsec and its age near 13.8 billion years; the 1998 supernova surveys, ground and space together, that revealed accelerating expansion driven by dark energy; atmospheres of planets around other stars. NASA framed Hubble as one of four Great Observatories spanning the spectrum: the Compton Gamma Ray Observatory launched in 1991, the Chandra X-ray Observatory in 1999, imaging million-degree gas and black-hole environments with half-arcsecond sharpness, and the infrared Spitzer Space Telescope in 2003. Beyond them, a fleet: the exoplanet counter Kepler from 2009, whose transit photometry showed planets outnumber stars; ESA's Gaia from 2013, mapping nearly two billion stars' positions and motions; and gravitational-wave and neutrino observatories opening non-electromagnetic windows entirely.

The generation-defining successor aimed at the infrared, where the earliest galaxies' light has been stretched by cosmic expansion and where planets and dust glow. The James Webb Space Telescope, a partnership of NASA, ESA and the Canadian Space Agency, launched on an Ariane 5 from Kourou on 25 December 2021, after decades of development and cost growth to roughly ten billion dollars. Too large for any rocket fairing in one piece, its 6.5-meter primary mirror is a mosaic of eighteen gold-coated beryllium hexagons that unfolded in flight, behind a tennis-court-sized five-layer sunshield, at the second Lagrange point 1.5 million kilometers from Earth, beyond any servicing. Every one of its 344 single-point deployments worked. Its first images, released on 12 July 2022, showed galaxies from the universe's first few hundred million years, and it has since delivered spectra of exoplanet atmospheres and infant galaxies more mature than models predicted, precisely the kind of productive surprise for which telescopes are built.

sections.heading: Segmented Mirrors, Adaptive Optics and Today's Giant Telescopes
sections.body:
For forty years after Palomar, ground-based astronomy seemed stuck near the five-meter mark: a bigger rigid mirror meant crippling weight, and the Soviet six-meter BTA of 1975, plagued by thermal problems, looked like proof of a ceiling. Two ideas broke it. The first was active optics, making mirrors thin, light and deliberately floppy, their shape corrected continuously by computer-controlled actuators against gravity and temperature; pioneered on the European Southern Observatory's 3.5-meter New Technology Telescope in 1989, it made monolithic mirrors of eight meters practical, spin-cast in a rotating furnace by Roger Angel's Arizona lab or polished from thin menisci for ESO's Very Large Telescope, four 8.2-meter units on Cerro Paranal in Chile, operational from 1998 to 2000.

The second idea abandoned the monolith. Jerry Nelson of the University of California designed a primary of many small hexagonal segments, each independently supported and positioned by sensors and actuators to act as one continuous surface, an engineering gamble realized in the two 10-meter Keck telescopes on Mauna Kea, Hawaii, with 36 segments each, Keck I observing from 1993 and Keck II from 1996. Segmentation made aperture scalable: the 10.4-meter Gran Telescopio Canarias followed in 2009, and every next-generation giant is segmented. Keck's twins also demonstrated that observatories had become computers with glass attached, queue-scheduled, remotely operated, their images assembled in software.

Software, in fact, conquered the atmosphere itself. Adaptive optics measures the turbulence-crumpled wavefront of a bright reference star hundreds of times per second and cancels the crumpling with a small deformable mirror; where no bright star sits near the target, a sodium laser fired from the telescope excites an artificial star in the mesosphere ninety kilometers up. Proposed by Horace Babcock in 1953 and matured through declassified defense technology in the 1990s, adaptive optics now routinely gives large ground telescopes sharper infrared images than Hubble. Its showcase result is decades of adaptive-optics astrometry at Keck and the VLT tracking stars whipping around the Milky Way's center, proving a black hole of about four million solar masses, the work recognized by the 2020 Nobel Prize to Andrea Ghez and Reinhard Genzel.

The present generation pushes both ideas to their limits. The European Southern Observatory's Extremely Large Telescope, rising on Cerro Armazones in Chile, will carry a 39.3-meter primary of 798 segments, gathering more light than every previous large optical telescope combined, with first light planned for the late 2020s; the Giant Magellan Telescope pairs seven 8.4-meter honeycomb mirrors into a 25.4-meter aperture; the Thirty Meter Telescope remains delayed amid disputes over construction on Mauna Kea, a reminder that observatories occupy mountains that are also other people's sacred and sovereign places. Survey astronomy, meanwhile, has its own flagship: the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile, whose 8.4-meter telescope and three-billion-pixel camera, the largest ever built, released first images in June 2025 and will photograph the entire southern sky every few nights for a decade, turning the sky into a searchable movie of moving and exploding things.

Four centuries separate Lipperhey's three-power spyglass from a 39-meter segmented eye watched over by lasers, yet the through-line is unbroken: every generation's telescope is a bet that gathering more light, a little more sharply, will show a universe stranger than the one expected. The bet has paid every single time.

guides.safetyNote: Never look at the Sun through any telescope, binoculars or finder scope without a purpose-made solar filter that covers the front of the instrument; magnified sunlight can permanently blind an eye in a fraction of a second, faster than you can blink or react. Small screw-in eyepiece solar filters sold with some cheap telescopes are dangerous, since concentrated heat can crack them in use, and eclipse glasses are for naked-eye viewing only, never for looking through optics. Use only full-aperture solar film or glass filters from reputable makers, check them for pinholes and scratches before every session, and cap or remove the finder so nobody, especially a child, glances through it while the telescope is aimed anywhere near the Sun.
